# Type: Integer and numeric {#sec-numeric}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
The machine version of discrete and continuous number
:::

Programs are to calculate, the natural object that you can create, store, and manipulate are numbers. There are two types of numbers following the concepts in mathematics @sec-discrete_continuous and in statistics @sec-quantitative-variable.

Discrete variables (or whole number) are represented by integer--truenoymy (vs mysnomy) used for counting and indexing.

In R programming, a real number (continuous) is called numeric.


While it is important to know these distinctions, in general R is very relaxed about the two types, and say smart enough that it would complain if you  mistakenly use that is supposed to be an integer. For instance, you can use numeric to specific the length of a vector, or as indexing.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
To force R to read a number as integer, we add L after the number

```{r}
my_favorite_integer <- 24L

```

A numeric is generally a number with decimals. The decimal separator in programming language (Excel is not a programming language) is a period "." Comma is used as a list separator (see @sec-vector, @sec-matrixCoding, and @sec-list).


```{r}
a_real_number <- 24.022
```


If the L is not specificed, R automatically assume that the value is numeric

```{r}
my_favorite_integer <- 24

```

## Examples {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| echo: true

# some constants are directly implemented/have their own notation
pi

# the square root of two is a numeric
sqrt(2)

# assign a number
my_number <- 2.13

a <- 2L
cc <- 2

# The function str here assess the type of the object. Here it is an integer
str(a)

# Here we show that the object is a numeric
str(cc)
```

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Concatenate: in the example below, we force R to add an integer and numeric. R chose to collapse to the more flexible format.

- An integer takes less memory in the computer. However, memory is not usually an issue and managing memory is beyond for now. We might return when one wants to optimize the code.
-  `r a <- .234` is a shortcut instead of `r a <- 0.234`
- Machine precision: there is a limit with the number of decimals. By default it is 16 decimal point. In data science it is extremely efficient.


```{r}
.Machine
```


- Astronomically big numbers are not allowed and again hopefully you won't need it.
- Due to precision, it is not good to multiply very small and very large number.
- Infinity is not a number and is represented by `Inf` and `-Inf`
